section_summary: This section covers diplomatic reporting and departmental analysis regarding Japanese political, economic, and foreign affairs during June 1933, primarily comprising Tokyo Embassy Despatch No. 459 (dated July 6, 1933) and an analytical summary memorandum by the State Department's Division of Far Eastern Affairs (dated August 8, 1933). The materials appear across four subfiles: the final pages of the Far Eastern Affairs memorandum (pages 161–163), a quadruplicate/carbon copy of Despatch No. 459 containing an executive summary, transmittal letter, monthly report, and lists of despatches/telegrams (pages 164–213), the complete Far Eastern Affairs memorandum (pages 214–219), and the official record copy of Despatch No. 459 running through Section II(c) (pages 220–240). Major subjects include improving Japanese-American relations marked by visits of Bishop Perry, Admiral Taylor, and Governor General Murphy, discussions of a proposed bilateral arbitration treaty, sharp commercial conflict with Great Britain leading to a Japanese boycott of Indian raw cotton, Tokyo negotiations over the Soviet sale of the Chinese Eastern Railway, extraterritoriality talks in Manchukuo, factional friction between Generals Ugaki and Araki, and domestic communist arrests.

subfiles.about: Concluding pages of a State Department Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum analyzing Tokyo Despatch No. 459 on conditions in Japan for June 1933.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs (initials LES / Laurence E. Salisbury)
subfiles.summary: Concluding memo on Despatch 459 covers Japan-Manchukuo extraterritoriality talks, Rea's Washington mission, an Ethiopian prince seeking a Japanese bride, Seiyukai dissent over Saito, Ugaki-Araki antagonism, Tokugawa's rumored Privy Seal appointment, exchange stability, and 400 Kyoto communist arrests.
subfiles.title: State Department Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 459 (Concluding Pages)

subfiles.about: U.S. Embassy Tokyo Despatch No. 459 transmitting the monthly report on political, foreign, and economic conditions in Japan for June 1933, with an executive summary and despatch lists.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, United States Ambassador to Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew transmits the Tokyo Embassy's comprehensive monthly political report for June 1933, accompanied by an executive summary, table of contents, and schedule of Embassy despatches and telegrams sent during the month. The report documents a noticeable warming in Japanese attitudes toward the United States prompted by high-profile goodwill visits (Bishop Perry, Admiral Taylor, Governor General Murphy) and Viscount Ishii's talks in Washington, despite lingering press criticism regarding American naval base construction and loans to China. It also details mounting trade friction with Great Britain culminating in a Japanese boycott of Indian raw cotton, Tokyo negotiations over the Soviet sale of the Chinese Eastern Railway, an alleged Soviet attack on Japanese fishermen off Kamchatka, and extraterritoriality talks in Hsinking. Domestically, the report examines Seiyukai party maneuvering against the Saito Cabinet, the bitter rivalry between Generals Ugaki and Araki, 1934–1935 military and naval budget proposals, record-low interest rates, and police crackdowns on communists including the Kyoto Imperial University incident.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 459: Monthly Report on Conditions in Japan During the Month of June, 1933 (Copy with Summary and Enclosures)
subfiles.to: Cordell Hull, Secretary of State, Washington

subfiles.about: State Department Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum providing an analytical summary of Tokyo Despatch No. 459 for departmental officials.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs (initials LES / Laurence E. Salisbury)
subfiles.summary: This six-page memorandum from the Division of Far Eastern Affairs synthesizes the principal findings of Ambassador Grew's June 1933 report on Japan for senior State Department officials. It reviews improving Japanese sentiment toward the United States while noting lingering suspicions regarding U.S. credit to China, press attacks on American naval expansion, and Japanese media reactions to the London Economic Conference. It outlines trade tensions with the British Empire leading to the upcoming Simla and London negotiations, the status of talks for the sale of the Chinese Eastern Railway, and Manchukuo extraterritoriality. In domestic affairs, it highlights the failed reconciliation between Generals Ugaki and Araki, Prince Tokugawa's resignation from the House of Peers, Mitsui's reorientation toward domestic industry, and widespread communist arrests among Kyoto students.
subfiles.title: State Department Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 459 (Complete Text)

subfiles.about: Official record copy of Ambassador Grew's Despatch No. 459 transmitting the June 1933 monthly report on conditions in Japan, extending through Section II(c).
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, United States Ambassador to Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: This document is the official departmental record copy of Tokyo Despatch No. 459, complete with departmental receipt and routing stamps, report cover page, index, and the first sixteen pages of the monthly report (ending mid-sentence in Section II(c)). The text examines the notable resurgence of goodwill toward the United States, highlighting the visits of Bishop James DeWolf Perry, Admiral Montgomery M. Taylor on the U.S.S. Houston, and Governor General Frank Murphy, as well as press discussions surrounding a prospective Japanese-American arbitration treaty. It covers Japanese diplomatic responses to President Roosevelt's world peace appeal, diplomatic efforts regarding the kidnapping of missionary Dr. Niels Nielsen in Manchuria, and denials of Kojiro Matsukata's rumored appointment as ambassador to Washington. Finally, it reviews Japan's policy at the London World Economic Conference, the Privy Council's conditional ratification of the international tariff truce, and the outbreak of severe commercial conflict with Great Britain following tariff hikes in India and the retaliatory raw cotton boycott instituted by the Japan Cotton Spinners' Association.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 459: Monthly Report on Conditions in Japan during the Month of June, 1933 (Record Copy, Sections I–II(c))
subfiles.to: Cordell Hull, Secretary of State, Washington
